I’ll start the new folks out with a referral recommendation of my own: Joseph Heath ‘s “ In Due Course ” substack is worth your time. Prof. Heath, a Canadian political scientist, posts with low frequency but consistently high quality about how and why human institutions, cultures, and interactions get screwed up and how to make them better. Two personal favorites of mine are Populism fast and slow and The Outliers . He is one of those rare people who I often disagree with but find reading him especially fruitful when I most strongly disagree.
He also wrote a book in 2014 called E

...

compelling. I read it last month and it’s by a long shot the most interesting and useful nonfiction I’ve read in the past year or two.
My brief and probably biased summary of Heath’s main points is:
* Enlightenment thinkers were right about the centrality of reason to human progress but wrong about the strength of the human capacity to reason.
* Conservative critics of the Enlightenment were right about the weakness of our reasoning capacity but wrong about why it’s weak and what to do about it.

He is the author of numerous academic and popular works, including Filthy Lucre , The Efficient Society , and (with Andrew Potter) The Rebel Sell . Heath received a Trudeau fellowship in 2012. He lives in Toronto.

BIO

Joseph Heath is a Canadian philosopher. He is a professor of Philosophy and the School of Public Policy and Governance at the University of Toronto, where he was formerly the director of the Centre for Ethics.
Heath is the author of several books, both popular and academic. His most recent, Morality, Competition and the Firm (Oxford, 2014), is a collection of papers on business ethics and the normative foundations of market economies. Enlightenment 2.0 (HarperCollins, 2014) is a call for a return to a more rational political discourse. Filthy Lucre (HarperCollins, 2009) is an analysis of economic fallacies and the role that they play in popular political discourse. Following the Rules (Oxford University Press, 2008), reflects on the phenomenon of rule-following and its significance for rationality and social interaction.
